newsitem.title: JAMAICA: Caricom delays Cuba trade accord again.
newsitem.headline: Caricom delays Cuba trade accord again.

text.p: Despite expectations to the contrary, Caribbean Community (Caricom) leaders delayed making a final decision on starting talks on a free trade accord with Cuba, officials said Thursday.
"There are political considerations involved in signing this treaty," Jamaica's industry minister Paul Robertson said.
Leaders of the 14-member grouping went into their summit at the Jamaican resort of Montego Bay having committed themselves to addressing the issue this week.
But a Caricom spokesman said they would now await the findings of a study to be presented to the next Caricom-Cuba joint commission meeting in December in Havana.
The free trade accord proposal was first put forward by Cuba two years ago and the Cubans are becoming "visibly annoyed" with the delays, according to one regional official.
A possible negative reaction from Washington, which maintains an economic embargo against the communist-ruled island, was a factor in Caricom thinking, the official added.
But Cuban Foreign Trade Minister Ricardo Cabrisas Ruiz said he did not believe political consequences were forcing the region to hold back from signing the proposed treaty.
"I would say our joint process has made a lot of headway. There are many issues to be considered; these things sometimes take years and so it doesn't have to happen at this session."
He said that six years ago, total trade between Caricom and Cuba stood at US$5 million-$6 million while last year the total was US$56 million. The figure this year is expected to be even larger.
Officials also say the differences between the free market economies of Caricom and the state-run economy in Cuba must first be dealt with.
"At this point in time, the Cuban economy is not such that we will benefit from a free trade accord," Jamaica's junior foreign trade minister Anthony Hylton said.

The underlying message is that Cuba first needs to open up its economy more. Grace Kennedy, one of the region's largest conglomerates, recently suspended its exports to Cuba for several months, citing problems with the bureaucracy of the state-owned trading houses.

"First of all, there is no credit so everything has to be cash up front," said Grace's managing director Douglas Orane. "You have to trade through the state-owned companies, and if they are late in payment there is little recourse except to sit and wait."

It is easier to export from Cuba than to import to Cuba. Caricom now enjoys a trade surplus with Cuba but trade officials said that if Trinidad's petroleum exports were removed, the surplus would be in Cuba's favor.

Statistics for Jamaica, Cuba's second-largest trade partner in Caricom, show that in 1995 Jamaica imported US$2.6 million worth of manufactured goods from Cuba. Jamaica's exports to Cuba in that same category were nil.
"We don't rule out that some bureaucracy may exist," Cabrisas said. Some problems were due to "a lack of knowledge of the business opportunities that exist."

The study to be ready in December is carried out by the European Union-funded, Barbados-based Caribbean Export Development Agency, which has opened an office in Havana to encourage more trade with Cuba.

The region remains committed to strengthening ties with Cuba in the long run. Five Caricom leaders have made official visits to Havana over the past year and several more will make the trip in the coming months.

Caricom took the opportunity of the May summit in Barbados with U.S. president Bill Clinton to seek to persuade him that its policy of "constructive engagement" with Havana would be more productive than Washington's attempts to isolate it.
Cuban President Fidel Castro is expected to attend next year's summit as part of the 25th anniversary celebrations of the regional integration movement.
